fields.title: e.g. Outbound damage below 0.30%
fields.owner: e.g. Anna K., Area Manager outbound
fields.how: e.g. Damage rate per week from the Damage Control log, on the control chart
fields.result: e.g. 0.31% in the two weeks after the roll-out, ten days below the old centre line
fields.countermeasure: A change to the process, not a reminder

background.title: Background
background.question: Why does this problem matter to the customer and the business, now?
background.placeholder: Two or three sentences: the context, who is affected, why now.

current.title: Current condition
current.question: What, where, since when, how much? Facts and numbers, no causes and no solutions yet.
current.placeholder: e.g. Over the last three weeks, 0.57% of outbound units left the hub damaged (104 of 18,400 in the last week) against 0.30% promised. Credits cost about €1,150 a week.

target.title: Target condition
target.question: What does good look like, measured how, by when, and what must not get worse?
target.placeholder: e.g. 0.30% or lower within eight weeks, without longer loading times.

cause.title: Root-cause analysis
cause.question: Why does the gap exist? Go to the floor, ask why until you reach something in the process you can change.
cause.placeholder: The chain of whys and the root cause at the end. A person is never the root cause: ask why it was possible.

countermeasures.title: Countermeasures
countermeasures.question: Which change to the process removes the root cause? One owner and one date each.

plan.title: Plan
plan.question: Who does what, in which order, by when? Pilot first, then roll out.

followUp.title: Follow-up
followUp.question: How and when will you check that the target condition holds, and what did you find?

number: Put a number in the current condition
time: The problem has a time frame
Say since when, or for which weeks
targetNumber: Give the target as a number
targetDate: Say by when the target holds
cause: The root cause is in the process
Name a root cause in the process, not a person
dates: Give every countermeasure a due date
measure: Say which number you will check, and where

tips: If it does not fit, you do not understand it yet. Cut words, not facts.
Current condition is facts and numbers.
What, where, since when, how much. No opinions and no solutions in box 2; they belong in boxes 4 and 5.
A reminder, a training or a warning letter is not a countermeasure. Change what the work makes possible.
Agree how and when you will check before you start. An A3 without box 7 is a plan, not a result.

example.title: Outbound damage below 0.30%
example.background: The hub ships about 18,400 units a week. Customers complain about crushed parcels, and the damage rate is almost twice what the contract promises. The credits and the complaints land on the Area Manager's desk every Monday.
example.current: Over the last three weeks, 0.57% of outbound units left the hub damaged (104 of 18,400 in the last week) against 0.30% promised to the customer. Credits cost about €1,150 a week. Pareto of the damage log: stacking 56%, load securing 14%, handling 11%; three causes carry 81%. Damage per 1,000 units is 2.4 times higher in the peak loading slots than in the others.
example.target: 0.30% or lower within eight weeks, without longer loading times: the loading-time target stays at 38 minutes per route.
example.rootCause:
Why is damage high? Parcels are crushed in the vehicle.
Why? Heavy parcels sit on top of light ones.
Why? In the late wave the loaders build the walls fast and fill gaps with whatever is at hand.
Why? There is no stacking rule at the dock, and the loading-time target wins over the stacking order.
Why? The standard was never written down: everybody is supposed to know how to stack.
Root cause: no visible stacking standard at the dock, and a loading-time target that rewards speed over a stable wall.

countermeasures.text: One stacking picture at every dock door: heavy low, fragile high, no gaps
Floor zones in the vehicle for heavy parcels, marked on the floor and in the loading plan
Locking bars after the last wall, with a photo before the doors close
Ten more minutes for the peak loading slots in the plan

plan.step: Pilot on docks 1 to 3, late shift
Train both shifts on the stacking picture: 15 minutes at the briefing
Daily p-chart of damage at the dock; a signal opens 5 Whys within 24 hours
Hand over to the outbound manager as the standard

example.how: Damage rate per week from the Damage Control log (damaged units ÷ units shipped) on the control chart; loading time per route from the route plan.
example.result: Damage fell from 0.57% to 0.31% (62 of 20,000 units in the two weeks after the roll-out), ten days in a row below the old centre line. Loading time rose by two minutes per route: accepted by the sponsor. Credits about €500 a week lower.
